Introduction to JavaScript

Beginner ⏱️ 5 min read Updated: July 2026

JavaScript is a versatile, high-level programming language that conforms to the ECMAScript specification. Alongside HTML and CSS, it is one of the core technologies of the World Wide Web.

Where does JavaScript run?

  • Client-Side: JavaScript runs in the user's web browser, allowing for interactive web pages.
  • Server-Side: With environments like Node.js, JavaScript can also run on servers to build robust backend systems.

Adding JavaScript to HTML

There are multiple ways to include JavaScript in your HTML documents:

1. Inline JavaScript
<button onclick="alert('Hello!')">Click Me</button>
2. Internal JavaScript
<script>
  console.log("Hello from Internal JS!");
</script>
3. External JavaScript (Recommended)
<!-- Include script at the end of body or use defer -->
<script src="main.js" defer></script>

topics.title: Variables & Data Types
topics.content:
Tutorials > Web Development > JavaScript > Basics

Variables & Data Types

Beginner ⏱️ 8 min read Updated: July 2026

Variables are containers for storing data values. In modern JavaScript, we use let and const for variable declaration.

var, let, and const

Keyword Scope Reassignable Hoisted
var Function scope Yes Yes
let Block scope Yes No (TDZ)
const Block scope No No (TDZ)

💡 Pro Tip

Always use const by default. Only use let if you know the variable's value will change (e.g., in a loop counter). Avoid using var in modern code.

Primitive Data Types

// 1. String
const name = "John Doe";

// 2. Number (includes integers and floats)
const age = 30;
const price = 99.99;

// 3. Boolean
const isLoggedIn = true;

// 4. Undefined (variable declared but not assigned)
let undefinedVar;

// 5. Null (intentional absence of any object value)
const emptyValue = null;

// 6. Symbol (unique identifier)
const sym = Symbol("id");

// 7. BigInt (for very large numbers)
const largeNumber = 9007199254740991n;

topics.title: Operators
topics.content:
Tutorials > Web Development > JavaScript > Basics

JavaScript Operators

Beginner ⏱️ 7 min read Updated: July 2026

Operators allow you to perform tests and mathematical operations on variables and values.

Arithmetic Operators

let a = 10;
let b = 3;

console.log(a + b);  // 13 (Addition)
console.log(a - b);  // 7  (Subtraction)
console.log(a * b);  // 30 (Multiplication)
console.log(a / b);  // 3.3333333333333335 (Division)
console.log(a % b);  // 1  (Modulus - Remainder)
console.log(a ** b); // 1000 (Exponentiation)

Comparison Operators (== vs ===)

The double equal (==) checks for equality of value, while the triple equal (===) checks for equality of both value and type.

console.log(5 == "5");  // true  (type coercion occurs)
console.log(5 === "5"); // false (different types: number vs string)
console.log(5 != "5");  // false
console.log(5 !== "5"); // true

Logical & Ternary Operators

// Logical AND (&&), OR (||), NOT (!)
const isAdult = true;
const hasId = false;

console.log(isAdult && hasId); // false
console.log(isAdult || hasId); // true
console.log(!isAdult);         // false

// Ternary Operator (condition ? exprIfTrue : exprIfFalse)
const age = 20;
const beverage = (age >= 21) ? "Beer" : "Juice";
console.log(beverage); // "Juice"

topics.title: Functions & Arrow Functions
topics.content:
Tutorials > Web Development > JavaScript > Functions

Functions & Arrow Functions

Essential ⏱️ 8 min read Updated: July 2026

A JavaScript function is a block of code designed to perform a particular task. It is executed when "something" invokes (calls) it.

1. Function Declaration

Function declarations are hoisted, meaning they can be called before they are defined in the code.

function greet(name) {
  return "Hello " + name + "!";
}

console.log(greet("Alice")); // Output: Hello Alice!

2. Function Expression

A function can also be defined inside an expression. These are not hoisted.

const multiply = function(a, b) {
  return a * b;
};

console.log(multiply(4, 5)); // Output: 20

3. Arrow Functions (ES6)

Arrow functions provide a shorter syntax and don't bind their own this context.

Arrow Function Syntax
// Standard arrow function
const add = (a, b) => {
  return a + b;
};

// Implicit return (single line)
const subtract = (a, b) => a - b;

// Single parameter (parentheses are optional)
const square = x => x * x;

💡 When to use Arrow Functions?

Use arrow functions for short callbacks (e.g., in array methods like map, filter) and when you need to preserve the lexical this context.

topics.title: Arrays & Array Methods
topics.content:
Tutorials > Web Development > JavaScript > Data Structures

Arrays & Array Methods

Essential ⏱️ 10 min read Updated: July 2026

Arrays are special variables that can hold more than one value at a time. JavaScript arrays are zero-indexed and can store mixed data types.

Basic Array Operations

const fruits = ["Apple", "Banana", "Orange"];

// Accessing elements
console.log(fruits[0]); // "Apple"

// Modifying elements
fruits[1] = "Mango";

// Length property
console.log(fruits.length); // 3

// Adding/Removing elements
fruits.push("Grape");    // Adds to the end
fruits.pop();            // Removes from the end
fruits.unshift("Kiwi");  // Adds to the beginning
fruits.shift();          // Removes from the beginning

Higher-Order Array Methods

Modern JavaScript relies heavily on functional array methods that iterate over elements.

Method Description Returns
map() Creates a new array populated with the results of calling a provided function on every element. New Array
filter() Creates a new array with all elements that pass the test implemented by the provided function. New Array
reduce() Executes a reducer function on each element, resulting in a single output value. Single Value
forEach() Executes a provided function once for each array element. undefined
Map, Filter, Reduce Example
const numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5];

// map: Double the numbers
const doubled = numbers.map(num => num * 2);
// [2, 4, 6, 8, 10]

// filter: Keep only even numbers
const evens = numbers.filter(num => num % 2 === 0);
// [2, 4]

// reduce: Sum all numbers
const sum = numbers.reduce((accumulator, current) => accumulator + current, 0);
// 15

topics.title: Objects & 'this' Keyword
topics.content:
Tutorials > Web Development > JavaScript > Data Structures

Objects & the 'this' Keyword

Core Concept ⏱️ 9 min read Updated: July 2026

Objects are collections of key-value pairs. They are the most important data type in JavaScript for storing structured data.

Creating and Accessing Objects

const user = {
  firstName: "Jane",
  lastName: "Doe",
  age: 25,
  isAdmin: false
};

// Dot notation
console.log(user.firstName); // "Jane"

// Bracket notation (useful for dynamic keys)
const key = "lastName";
console.log(user[key]); // "Doe"

// Adding/Modifying properties
user.email = "jane@example.com";
user.age = 26;

Object Methods & 'this'

Functions stored as object properties are called methods. The this keyword refers to the object executing the current function.

⚠️ Arrow Functions and 'this'

Arrow functions do not have their own this binding. They inherit this from the enclosing lexical scope. Therefore, do not use arrow functions as object methods if you need to access object properties via this.

const person = {
  name: "Bob",
  greet: function() {
    // 'this' refers to the person object
    return `Hello, my name is ${this.name}`;
  },
  // Shorthand syntax (ES6)
  sayBye() {
    return `Goodbye from ${this.name}`;
  },
  // BAD: Arrow function for method
  badGreet: () => {
    return `Hi, I am ${this.name}`; // this.name will be undefined!
  }
};

console.log(person.greet()); // "Hello, my name is Bob"

topics.title: DOM Manipulation
topics.content:
Tutorials > Web Development > JavaScript > DOM & Events

DOM Manipulation

Browser API ⏱️ 8 min read Updated: July 2026

The Document Object Model (DOM) is a programming interface for web documents. It represents the page so that programs can change the document structure, style, and content.

Selecting Elements

Method Description
getElementById("id") Returns a single element with the matching ID.
querySelector(".class") Returns the first element matching the CSS selector.
querySelectorAll("div") Returns a NodeList of all elements matching the selector.

Modifying Content & Styles

// 1. Select the element
const heading = document.querySelector("#main-title");

// 2. Change Text
heading.textContent = "New Title Updated via JS!";

// 3. Change HTML
const box = document.querySelector(".box");
box.innerHTML = "<strong>Bold Text!</strong>";

// 4. Change Styles
heading.style.color = "#10b981";
heading.style.fontSize = "3rem";
heading.style.display = "none"; // Hide element

Creating and Appending Elements

// Create a new paragraph
const newPara = document.createElement("p");
newPara.textContent = "I was created dynamically.";
newPara.classList.add("text-muted");

// Append it to a container
const container = document.getElementById("content-div");
container.appendChild(newPara);

topics.title: Event Listeners
topics.content:
Tutorials > Web Development > JavaScript > DOM & Events

Event Listeners

Interactive ⏱️ 7 min read Updated: July 2026

JavaScript can execute code when events occur (like clicking a button, typing in a field, or loading a page). We use the addEventListener method to attach event handlers to elements.

addEventListener Syntax
element.addEventListener(event, function, useCapture);

Common Events

  • Mouse: click, dblclick, mouseenter, mouseleave
  • Keyboard: keydown, keyup, keypress
  • Form: submit, change, input, focus
  • Window: load, resize, scroll

Event Listener Example

const btn = document.querySelector("#submit-btn");

btn.addEventListener("click", function(event) {
  // Prevent default form submission behavior if needed
  event.preventDefault();
  
  // 'event.target' refers to the element that triggered the event
  event.target.style.backgroundColor = "green";
  event.target.textContent = "Clicked!";
  
  console.log("Button was clicked at coordinates:", event.clientX, event.clientY);
});

💡 Event Delegation

Instead of adding listeners to multiple child elements (like list items), add a single listener to their parent element and check event.target. This is more efficient and handles dynamically added children.

topics.title: Asynchronous JavaScript
topics.content:
Tutorials > Web Development > JavaScript > Advanced

Asynchronous JavaScript: Promises & Async/Await

Advanced ⏱️ 12 min read Updated: July 2026

JavaScript is single-threaded. To prevent blocking the main thread during long operations (like fetching data from an API), JavaScript uses asynchronous patterns.

1. Promises

A Promise is an object representing the eventual completion or failure of an asynchronous operation.

const myPromise = new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
  let success = true;
  
  setTimeout(() => {
    if(success) {
      resolve("Data fetched successfully!");
    } else {
      reject("Error fetching data.");
    }
  }, 2000);
});

myPromise
  .then(result => console.log(result))
  .catch(error => console.error(error))
  .finally(() => console.log("Operation complete."));

2. Fetch API

The fetch() method is a modern way to make network requests. It returns a Promise.

fetch('https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/users/1')
  .then(response => {
    if (!response.ok) throw new Error("Network error");
    return response.json(); // Parses JSON and returns another promise
  })
  .then(data => console.log("User Name:", data.name))
  .catch(error => console.error("Fetch Error:", error));

3. Async / Await (ES8)

async/await is syntactic sugar on top of Promises, making asynchronous code look and behave a little more like synchronous code.

Async/Await Example
async function getUserData() {
  try {
    const response = await fetch('https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/users/1');
    if (!response.ok) {
      throw new Error(`HTTP error! status: ${response.status}`);
    }
    const data = await response.json();
    console.log("User:", data);
  } catch (error) {
    console.error("Error occurred:", error);
  }
}

getUserData();

topics.title: ES6+ Features
topics.content:
Tutorials > Web Development > JavaScript > Advanced

Modern JavaScript (ES6+ Features)

Modern JS ⏱️ 10 min read Updated: July 2026

ECMAScript 2015 (ES6) and subsequent versions introduced powerful new syntax and features that make writing JavaScript easier and cleaner.

1. Destructuring Assignment

Unpack values from arrays or properties from objects into distinct variables.

// Object Destructuring
const user = { name: "Alice", age: 28, city: "Paris" };
const { name, city } = user;
console.log(name, city); // "Alice Paris"

// Array Destructuring
const colors = ["Red", "Green", "Blue"];
const [primary, secondary] = colors;
console.log(primary); // "Red"

2. Spread & Rest Operators (...)

// Spread (Expand arrays/objects)
const arr1 = [1, 2];
const arr2 = [...arr1, 3, 4]; // [1, 2, 3, 4]

const obj1 = { a: 1, b: 2 };
const obj2 = { ...obj1, c: 3 }; // { a: 1, b: 2, c: 3 }

// Rest (Gather remaining arguments into an array)
function sum(...numbers) {
  return numbers.reduce((acc, val) => acc + val, 0);
}
console.log(sum(1, 2, 3, 4)); // 10

3. Template Literals

Use backticks (`) to allow embedded expressions and multi-line strings.

const product = "Laptop";
const price = 999;

// ES5 way
const msg1 = "The " + product + " costs $" + price + ".";

// ES6 Template Literal
const msg2 = `The ${product} costs $${price}.`;

// Multi-line
const html = `
  <div>
    <h1>${product}</h1>
  </div>
`;
